name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: A Unified Gateway for Calling and Governing LLM APIs
answer: LiteLLM is an open source AI gateway from BerriAI that lets Python code and a proxy server call over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging. It sits between your application and providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure, and Vertex AI. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its Python proxy has a history of memory and cost regressions, and a Rust rewrite promising far lower overhead is still in early beta.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and distributed from the GitHub repository BerriAI/litellm under a custom licence. It is a Python library and an accompanying proxy server, described on its official site as the fastest, litest AI gateway, with a Rust core and a Python SDK. The repository's last recorded push is October 2, 2026, and it has around 60,061 stars. In the AI stack it occupies the gateway layer: it does not train models or serve weights itself, it sits between application code and model providers, translating requests into a common format and applying policy around them. The site lists support for Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM, and Nvidia NIM among more than 100 APIs.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are calling many providers through one interface, tracking spend, enforcing guardrails, balancing load across deployments, and logging traffic. The documentation shows batch_completion_models_all_responses sending one conversation to every model in parallel and returning only the responses that succeeded, which suits reliability testing across providers. The blog describes an Agent Gateway that authenticates callers and records request, response, latency, and cost data, a Model Gateway that routes LLM traffic and applies budgets and rate limits, and an MCP Gateway that centralizes tool access and upstream authentication. Budgets are supported at key, team, agent, and customer levels. It is strongest where a team needs one control plane over many providers, shared agents, and per-user attribution rather than raw model performance.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone comfortable with Python and HTTP APIs, since the basic pattern is a completion call with a provider-prefixed model name. The proxy, however, assumes real operational knowledge: Redis, Kubernetes, nginx, OIDC, OAuth2 authorization code flows with PKCE, and rate limiting concepts all appear in the official material. The site offers tutorials, including a reliability testing walkthrough, and blog posts that explain incidents in detail. A beginner can follow the quickstart, but running the gateway in production requires systems experience. The documentation does not present a structured curriculum, so a student should expect to learn by reading pages and experimenting rather than following a course.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: LiteLLM integrates with a long list of providers, including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM, and Nvidia NIM, and speaks the A2A JSON-RPC interface for agent calls. It supports OIDC and other credentials for user authentication, and MCP servers with auth_type oauth2 and oauth2_flow authorization_code for tool access. The site documents SSO/SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management, and guardrails. Community signals include roughly 60,061 GitHub stars and an active blog with tags for ai-gateway and incident-report. The documentation is the primary reference, and the blog functions as a changelog of both features and failures.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: The Python library is built for quick experiments: a few lines call a hosted model, and batch helpers fan out across providers. The proxy is aimed at production, with budgets, rate limits, caching, and logging, but the site is candid that the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load and that pods get OOM-killed at the worst time. The Rust gateway is presented as the production answer, serving about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, and cutting per-request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. That Rust gateway is an early beta, so the performance gain is not yet a settled default.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show an enterprise customer running litellm-database:v1.100.0 behind nginx, which indicates real production deployment at scale. The site describes features built for production, including SSO/SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management, and guardrails, and it names Portkey and Bifrost as gateways it benchmarks against. That places LiteLLM among current gateway choices rather than a legacy tool. For someone choosing what to learn, gateway skills transfer: provider abstraction, cost attribution, rate limiting, and identity propagation appear in the site's agent and FinOps material. The facts do not give adoption numbers beyond the star count and the named customer scenario, so claims about market share would be unsupported.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core, so it is typically used from Python applications, and its proxy is deployed as a service in front of other languages' code. It calls providers over HTTP via httpx rather than importing vendor SDKs, which the site notes in explaining why the compromised mistralai package never executes in a LiteLLM environment. It sits beside orchestration frameworks rather than replacing them, and it interoperates with MCP servers for tools and A2A for agent-to-agent calls. The polyglot pattern is a thin client in any language talking to the gateway, with the gateway holding provider credentials, budgets, and logs centrally.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site documents serious failures. A Medium severity incident saw two waves of kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61 GB RSS, and thousands of 502s, caused by unbounded retry breadcrumbs when Redis was unreachable. Another silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising spend 2-3x. The Rust gateway is an early beta, and the site says the migration aims for a pure Rust server serving 100% of traffic, which is not yet the state. The documentation does not state a stable release date for that migration, does not give independent benchmarks, and does not settle how the custom licence affects commercial use.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
